exercises.title: Return a value in the right place
exercises.brief: Write answer, a function taking no arguments that returns 42. The checks call it and compare what comes back.
exercises.concept: A function returns its value in rax because the calling convention says so, and nothing in the hardware enforces that.
hints: The return value goes in rax. The starter puts it somewhere else.

diagnose.prose: The checks read rax after calling you, because that is where the System V convention says a return value lives. Putting 42 in another register is not wrong in any way the processor can detect, which is exactly the point: the convention is a contract, and both sides have to keep it.
Read the line the assembler names. Intel syntax puts the destination first, and every instruction here needs a comma between its two operands.

exercises.after: Notice there is no type, no signature and no declaration. The agreement that rax holds the answer exists only in a document.
exercises.starter:
.intel_syntax noprefix
.text
.global answer
answer:
    mov rbx, 42
    ret
exercises.tests:
.global _start
_start:
    call answer
    cmp rax, 42
    jne fail
    mov edi, 0
    mov eax, 60
    syscall
fail:
    mov edi, 1
    mov eax, 60
    syscall

exercises.title: The width that clears the top
exercises.brief: clear_top is given a 64-bit value in rdi with every bit set. Return a value whose upper 32 bits are zero and whose lower 32 bits are 5, using a single move into the right name.
exercises.concept: Writing a 32-bit register name zero-extends into the full 64 bits. Writing a 16-bit name does not.
hints: The starter uses ax. There is a wider name for the same register.

diagnose.prose: Writing through ax changes 16 bits and leaves the other 48 exactly as they were, so the upper half of rdi survives into your answer. Writing through eax clears the upper 32 bits as a side effect. That asymmetry is the whole exercise, and it exists because zero-extension breaks the dependency on the register's previous value, which lets the processor start the instruction immediately.

exercises.after: The 8-bit and 16-bit forms behave the old way because code from 1985 depended on it. The 32-bit form was new in 2000 and could be defined freshly.
exercises.starter:
.intel_syntax noprefix
.text
.global clear_top
clear_top:
    mov rax, rdi
    mov ax, 5
    ret
exercises.tests:
.global _start
_start:
    mov rdi, -1
    call clear_top
    cmp rax, 5
    jne fail
    mov edi, 0
    mov eax, 60
    syscall
fail:
    mov edi, 1
    mov eax, 60
    syscall

exercises.title: Two values through the stack
exercises.brief: swap_diff takes two values in rdi and rsi. Push both, then pop them into the opposite registers, and return the first minus the second. With 30 and 12 the answer is negative 18.
exercises.concept: A stack reverses order, so pushing two values and popping two values swaps them.
hints: The last thing pushed is the first thing popped.

diagnose.prose: Work the stack by hand. After push rdi then push rsi, the top of the stack holds what was in rsi. So the first pop takes that one. The starter pops them back into the registers they came from, which swaps nothing.

exercises.after: push and pop are not stack instructions in any deep sense. They are sub rsp, 8 with a store, and a load with add rsp, 8.
exercises.starter:
.intel_syntax noprefix
.text
.global swap_diff
swap_diff:
    push rdi
    push rsi
    pop rsi
    pop rdi
    mov rax, rdi
    sub rax, rsi
    ret
exercises.tests:
.global _start
_start:
    mov rdi, 30
    mov rsi, 12
    call swap_diff
    cmp rax, -18
    jne fail
    mov edi, 0
    mov eax, 60
    syscall
fail:
    mov edi, 1
    mov eax, 60
    syscall

exercises.title: Which way is up
exercises.brief: second_from_top pushes three values and returns the middle one by reading it directly off the stack rather than popping. Clean the stack up before you return.
exercises.concept: The stack grows toward lower addresses, so the item below the top is at a higher address.
hints: After three pushes, [rsp] is the last one pushed. Count upward from there.

diagnose.prose: Draw the addresses. Each push subtracts 8 from rsp first, so after pushing a, b, c in that order, c is at [rsp], b is at [rsp + 8] and a is at [rsp + 16]. Subtracting from rsp reads memory the stack has not claimed yet.
The address you computed is not mapped. Reading below rsp by a large amount leaves the region the kernel gave you, which is a fault rather than garbage.

exercises.after: Reading past the end of a structure gives you whatever is next in memory and no complaint. Here it happened to be another value you had pushed.
exercises.starter:
.intel_syntax noprefix
.text
.global second_from_top
second_from_top:
    push rdi
    push rsi
    push rdx
    mov rax, [rsp - 8]
    add rsp, 24
    ret
exercises.tests:
.global _start
_start:
    mov rdi, 100
    mov rsi, 200
    mov rdx, 300
    call second_from_top
    cmp rax, 200
    jne fail
    mov edi, 0
    mov eax, 60
    syscall
fail:
    mov edi, 1
    mov eax, 60
    syscall

exercises.title: A name that is not there
exercises.brief: use_helper should return twice its argument by calling double_it, which the checks define for you. The starter calls something else. Read what the linker says rather than what the assembler says.
exercises.concept: An assembler accepts any name you write. The linker is what decides whether that name exists.
hints: The helper the checks provide is called double_it.

diagnose.prose:
Every line of your code assembled without complaint, because to an assembler a name it has not seen is just a name it has not seen yet. The linker went looking for the body and found nothing, and the message it gives names the symbol and the section offset that referred to it.

This failure looks different from a compile error in the tooling: nothing reports a build failure, and the result is simply that no executable was produced.
The name resolves now and the answer is wrong. double_it expects its argument in rdi and returns in rax, like everything else here.

exercises.after: Undefined symbols are the single most common build failure in C and C++ too, and they mean the same thing there: something promised a definition and nothing supplied one.
exercises.starter:
.intel_syntax noprefix
.text
.global use_helper
use_helper:
    call twice_it
    ret
exercises.tests:
.global double_it
double_it:
    mov rax, rdi
    add rax, rax
    ret

.global _start
_start:
    mov rdi, 21
    call use_helper
    cmp rax, 42
    jne fail
    mov edi, 0
    mov eax, 60
    syscall
fail:
    mov edi, 1
    mov eax, 60
    syscall

exercises.title: Put it back the way you found it
exercises.brief: uses_rbx may use rbx for its own working, and must leave it holding whatever it held on entry. Return the argument plus one.
exercises.concept: Callee-saved registers are the half of the file a function has to preserve, and nothing checks that it did.
hints: rbx is callee-saved. There is a two-instruction way to borrow it.

diagnose.prose: The checks put a known value in rbx, call you, and look at rbx afterwards. The starter overwrites it and never restores it. Push it on entry and pop it before the ret, and mind that the pop has to happen before the return rather than after it.
The stack is unbalanced. A push with no matching pop leaves rsp pointing at your saved value, so ret jumps to that value instead of to your caller.

exercises.after: This is why a compiler prefers caller-saved registers for short-lived values. Using rbx costs two instructions before you have done any work.
exercises.starter:
.intel_syntax noprefix
.text
.global uses_rbx
uses_rbx:
    mov rbx, rdi
    add rbx, 1
    mov rax, rbx
    ret
exercises.tests:
.global _start
_start:
    mov rbx, 0x1234
    mov rdi, 41
    call uses_rbx
    cmp rax, 42
    jne fail
    cmp rbx, 0x1234
    jne fail
    mov edi, 0
    mov eax, 60
    syscall
fail:
    mov edi, 1
    mov eax, 60
    syscall

exercises.title: Six arguments, in order
exercises.brief: sum_six takes six integers and returns their sum. The checks pass 1 through 6, so the answer is 21. Getting this wrong tells you which register you had in the wrong place.
exercises.concept: The first six integer arguments go in a fixed order, and the order is not alphabetical or numerical.

diagnose.prose:
Add the registers you used and see which sum you got. The starter stops after four, so it returns 10 rather than 21, which tells you exactly how many arguments it read.

The order is worth memorising because it is not guessable. rcx is the fourth argument for an ordinary call and is not used at all by the syscall interface, which puts r10 in its place, because the syscall instruction overwrites rcx with the return address.

exercises.after: Beyond six, arguments go on the stack, which is why a function with many parameters is measurably slower to call than one with few.
exercises.starter:
.intel_syntax noprefix
.text
.global sum_six
sum_six:
    mov rax, rdi
    add rax, rsi
    add rax, rdx
    add rax, rcx
    ret
exercises.tests:
.global _start
_start:
    mov rdi, 1
    mov rsi, 2
    mov rdx, 3
    mov rcx, 4
    mov r8, 5
    mov r9, 6
    call sum_six
    cmp rax, 21
    jne fail
    mov edi, 0
    mov eax, 60
    syscall
fail:
    mov edi, 1
    mov eax, 60
    syscall

exercises.title: Ending a program that has nowhere to return
exercises.brief: _start is the entry point and nothing called it, so there is no return address on the stack and ret has nothing to return to. Write the exit sequence yourself. A program that ends cleanly here exits with status 0.
exercises.concept: Without a C runtime underneath, a program ends by asking the kernel to end it.
hints: Syscall 60 is exit, and its one argument goes where the first argument always goes.

diagnose.prose: Running off the end of your code is a fault, and so is ret at _start, because the value it pops is whatever the kernel left on the stack rather than a return address. Neither is a bug in your logic; both are what happens when a program does not end deliberately.
It exited, with a nonzero status. The number in rax selects the syscall and the number in rdi is the status, so check you have not swapped them.

exercises.after: The status is one byte. Exit with 256 and the kernel reports 0, which has confused a great many test scripts.
